en: The Lamp of the Determination of Śambhu (Śambhunirṇayadīpikā), composed by Śivānandanātha. Auspiciousness!
I worship Śiva, whose nature is consciousness, who is all-pervasive, supremely noble, and resides within earth, water, milk, the great sun, wind, space, and the mind.
[This work was composed] by Pratiṣṭhānanda’s son, Ajeśaprabhu.
A concise commentary on the *Mata-īśa* is being written by Śivānanda. The Lord brought down this Tantra— which is all-gracious, which illuminates everything,
and which grants the perfection of all qualifications— for the sake of the complete attainment of all authorizations.
The omnipresent Lord Śambhu has taught many scriptures— some emphasizing ritual action, some emphasizing knowledge, and others that are a mixture of both.
These include the Mahāmata, the Lakṣamata, and the Mateśānamata.
Thus, by that [name], a great scripture was revealed under such titles as these.
Furthermore, due to the expansion of that scripture and out of his supreme compassion,
Śiva again condensed it into the *Śrīśāsana-sahasrārtha*.
The Lord Śrīśambhunirṇaya, known by the name Mateśa,
has spread throughout these worlds like the radiance of the sun;
he is indeed Śambhu himself manifest under the designation of Śrīcaryānātha.
Manifesting the scripture upon the earth, he stands in the position of a great guru;
established in his lineage is the illustrious one known by the name Pratiṣṭhānanda.
There was a certain yogi, Maheśāna by name, a teacher whose very form was composed of merit alone.
This yogi, Śivānanda Muni, was ever intent on meditation upon Śiva. Having seen that teacher in a dream, he subsequently beheld him again in person.
Having studied the scriptures from the mouth of his preceptor, preceded by the acquisition of specialized knowledge,
the great sage Śivānanda dwelt in the presence of his gurus.
After a long time, he was [honored] by those gurus, who were overflowing with compassion.
Having established him in the rite of grace, together with the consecration and the secret [teachings],
he then initiated his disciples, who were adorned by their conduct,
who knew the distinctions of place and time, and who were great oceans of the jewels of devotion.
At the request of the wise Cidānanda, a disciple who has served Śivānandamuni for a long time, he composed this commentary.
From the milky ocean of Pratiṣṭhānanda, the moon of Śivānanda has arisen.

The commentary *Śambhunirṇayadīpikā*, pregnant with devotion to the state of remembering the Guru and filled with the affection of a mind established in the *Sthālī* [tradition], has been clearly composed as a moonlight that spreads across the surface of the earth the explanation of the *Śrīsahasrārdha*.
The fault of being both hearer and listener does not fall within the range of their vision;
for we are indeed the commentators who illuminate faults in Śiva. Indeed, there is no treatise anywhere in this world that speaks of faults [in Him].
A fault may arise anywhere through either negligence or lack of independence;
the ignorant do not recognize such a fault, whereas the wise instruct them regarding it.
Therefore, some do not impute fault to the commentator.

In this regard, the illustrious *Sahasrārdhaśāsana* is intent upon establishing twenty-six topics and consists of that same number of sections. Among these, by the first section, the arrangement of the worship-mandala (*arcāmaṇḍala*) is taught; by the second, the synonyms for worship; by the third, the worship of the nine lords (*naveśvara*); by the fourth, the worship of the female messengers (*dūtī*); by the fifth, the fire-oblation (*homa*) of the nine lords; and by the sixth, the removal of the multitude of diseases.

By the seventh [chapter], the meditation on the glory of the manifestation (*śrīvaibhavadhyāna*). By the eighth, the meditation on Power (*śaktidhyāna*). By the ninth, the meditation on the moon (*aindavadhyāna*). By the tenth, the meditation on the sun (*prābhākaradhyāna*). By the eleventh, the sixteenfold seed-syllables (*bījaṣoḍhā*).

By the twelfth, the extraction of the *Śrīsamayāśambara*. By the thirteenth, the extraction of the *Kṣetreśaśambara*. By the fourteenth, the practice of the venerable [deity] (*śrīsādhana*). By the fifteenth, the wheel that bestows all desired objects (*sarvasamīhitaprada-cakra*).

By the sixteenth, the possession by the Virgin Goddess (*kumārikāveśa*). By the seventeenth, the worship of the venerable sequence (*śrīkramasaparyā*). By the eighteenth, the worship of the atoms (*paramāṇūnām arcanam*). By the nineteenth, the means for the expansion of the intellect (*mativikāsopāya*).

The twenty-second [chapter] concerns the *sādhana* of Śrī Śikheśvara; the twenty-first, the *nyāsa* of that [deity]’s seizing (*tadgraha*); the twenty-second, the agitation of the city (*purakṣobha*); the twenty-third, the yoga of Mṛtyuñjaya; the twenty-fourth, the transmigration for the sake of the next world (*pāralaukikasamutkrānti*); the twenty-fifth, the means for attaining bodily perfection (*śarīrasiddhi*); and the twenty-sixth, the yoga of the crest (*śikhāyoga*). This divine teaching is difficult to penetrate, extremely secret, and accessible only through the oral tradition (*sampradāya*); it is now explained exactly as it was heard from the mouth of the Guru.

We praise that Śiva who always shines through his own absolute freedom (svātantrya) as the one who possesses the nature of the sacrificial pit, the maṇḍala, initiation, the sequence of worship, the object of worship, and the worshipper himself. The two sūtras beginning with "svārājya" form a single syntactical unit.
Having bowed to that immutable Śambhu, who is the sovereign of his own kingdom, the Lord of Hāṭaka, and the means for attaining liberation while living, I, the daughter of Himavat, shall speak.
O Lord of the World, out of fear of prolixity, I ask you about a concise method for accomplishing the worship of the one whose self is Śiva—a worship that grants all desires of the mind.
By the word *sva* (one's own), which denotes heaven (*svarga*), *dharma* is indicated; by the word *rājya* (kingdom), *artha*; and by the word *hāṭakeśāna*, *kāma*. As it has been said:
"In some places he was protected by that Lord Hāṭakeśa, who desired the play of worshiping with infinite [offerings] gathered by the Asurīs. Thus it is said.

Liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) and liberation after death (*mṛtamukti*) are the means for the five [goals], beginning with *dharma*. For from Him, Śambhu—the one whose meaning is "the one who has crossed over" (*tīrṇa*) the ocean of existence (*bhava*)—these arise.

[He is] the bringer of bliss for practitioners. By this [statement], he indicates that even for the devotees (*upāsaka*), there is freedom from the constraints of time (*akālakalitatva*). And it has been said:
"He who always possesses this contemplation is liberated even while living;
he who constantly contemplates Śiva—time cannot overcome him."

Thus [it is said]. "Himātmajā" means the daughter of Himavat. "For fear of Vyāsa" means for fear of the extensive elaboration mentioned previously; the meaning is: for the sake of the ease of those who perform the practice. "Laghusādhyām" means that which is to be accomplished through a concise summary.

The construction is: "I ask you. O Lord of the World, O Protector of the Universe! "Saparyām" means worship. "Sarvacittecchādāyinīm" means the giver of all desires of the mind; or, the giver of the joy of all mental desires.

Or, "sarvecchādātrīm" refers to the heart (hṛdayam) in the sense of the locative case—within the heart of Śrīnivāsa, whose self is Śrī Śiva, wherein all desires, from sovereignty up to liberation, reside.
In the conscious Self, which is the locus of the foundation of the universe; as it has been said:
"One should know that [Self] to be the heart, the great abode of the universe.
Thus:
"Because of the friction of the mind within the heart, the visible world is one's own non-perception.

And also: "In the inner self (*svānta*), [the word] *svāntam* means the mind (*manas*) in the sense of the accusative case; having made it the cause for that which is included within the modifications (*vikāra*)," this is the ellipsis. "Make the mind [so]" means: "having fixed your attention, act [in such a way]."

"Place [it]," meaning "place it in the middle station. "Our word," meaning the beneficial words of instruction, [is] "in your heart," that is, in the mind. "May your divine perfections be [present]" means: taking you, who are the soul of the universe, as the instrumental cause, we instruct for the benefit of the three worlds. Therefore, for the best of practitioners who is intent on benefiting you and is vigilant, all the perfections—from *aṇimā* up to liberation—[shall be attained].

The meaning is "let them be. In this *Śambhunirṇayadīpikā*, we shall explain the very same meaning that was previously heard from the mouth of the Guru. This meaning has been accomplished by us, enduring the hardship of residing in the presence of the Guru. Because it is the word of the *Āgama*, the traditional meaning becomes even more extensive. "Previous entry" (*purāpraveśanam*): preceded by entry, [it refers to] the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), which consists of grace and is of the nature of the supreme sovereignty of Śakti.

The meaning is: being endowed with distinguished characteristics, having first received initiation from a guru through the traditional lineage (*sampradāya*). "Above all living beings" (*prāṇinām*)—the word *prāṇabhṛtām* (those who possess breath) is to be supplied as the remainder. "In every way, even in the state where life is being taken away, maintain [your] anger"—that is, having attained the stages of the rules (*samaya*) and so forth, such as the worship of the deity, one should perform the worship of the venerable Lord Śiva while maintaining the contemplation of Śiva everywhere and viewing the universe as oneself. And it has been said:
"If there is the assault of the senses, what is to be gained by the worship of the worshipful?"
"If there is no penetration by the senses, what is to be gained from honoring those worthy of worship?

And it is said: "If a person should kill a living being who has been initiated into the *Mahākāruṇika* scripture, then by that act, the rays of Śambhu are killed. The "attainment of all" (*sarvasiddhi*) consists of the pentad beginning with Dharma. It refers to the three means—Āṇava, Śākta, and Śāmbhava—which are proclaimed in the three commands (*ājñā*), characterized by the performance of the *udhāraka* and other rites, and whose sole embodiment is pure consciousness consisting of the activity of the mind.

"Having taken"—that is, having obtained—the initiation (*dīkṣā*) characterized by the bestowal of Śiva-nature and the destruction of the bonds (*pāśa*) through the process of differentiation; "the Guru" means he who imparts that [initiation] to the disciple, teaching its true meaning. Therefore, the meaning is: "having received initiation from a Guru until it culminates in his own personal experience.

Furthermore, "together with the consecration" (*sābhiṣekām*) means accompanied by the rite of consecration (*abhiṣeka*); "with a wife" (*sapatnīkām*) means together with a partner in dharma (*sahadharmacāriṇī*). "Then," that is, immediately after the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) characterized by the attainment of awakening, one should "resort to the performance" (*anuṣṭhānakaṃ bhajet*).

One should perform obligatory and occasional rites according to the prescribed rules. The grammatical connection is that one should worship after assuming the lotus posture (*padmāsana*). "The primordial form" refers to the morning [ritual]; by the word "primordial," the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) and so forth are indicated.

The meaning is that one whose body is purified by bathing and other means, having first performed the twilight worship of knowledge and so forth. As it has been said: "One who omits the twilight worship is perpetually impure and unfit for all ritual acts."
Thus [it is said]: "A secluded place, free from the gaze of the uninitiated (paśu). And it has been stated:
"In a temple or a house that is pure, pleasing, and free from the falling gaze of the uninitiated.

"Having recollected" means: that worshipper [recollects] first the Supreme, who is the worshipper of all, the abode of Śambhu (*śāmbhavaṃ dhāma*), the efflorescence of consciousness (*vittasamullāsa*), whose form vibrates everywhere and in every way; and therefore, whose nature is known by the agent.

Having recollected that supreme light, the highest light; and having contemplated all the deities as being of the nature of *kalā*s, one should place [the offering] upon the head along with its cause, at the *brahmarandhra* by means of the *nidāna*, for the sake of that supreme *dhāma*. Together with its cause, the flower is to be consumed. [One should offer] the *rasa* and *gandha*. The meaning is that, by means of the ultimate sense of the letter *pra*, it should be absorbed into the Supreme Subject, Paramaśiva. Half of the food and water—[that is,] half of the food.

"Half-watered": the word *ardha* is masculine here. "With its cause" means provided with the ritual procedure. "Accompanied by the gaze of the mantra" means by a glance endowed with the mantra. "Recited without extraction" means recited without [the removal of] the *muktaka*. "By the syllable of the bee" means by the sixteen-syllable [mantra]. "Bestowing all accomplishments" refers to the mantra that bestows the five groups; this is the ellipsis. "Enveloped by spirits and so forth" means surrounded by *bhūtas*, *yakṣas*, *rākṣasas*, and lords of the fields (*kṣetrādhipatis*). This is the meaning of these two lines.

The meaning of the sentence is as follows: Having placed a shared cup filled with food and water, and having meditated upon [the deity] surrounded by the Bhūtas and other attendants, one should offer the *śānti-bali* while reciting this sixteen-syllable mantra three times while casting a glance [at it]. He states the mantra for the offering:

*Oṃ hrīṃ sarvavighnakṛdbhyaḥ sarvabhūtebhyo hrūṃ svāhā*. Immediately after that performance of the *śānti-bali*, one should [recite] the verses concerning the maṇḍala in front of oneself—that is, in front of one's own worshipper.

Five *praṇavas* [are used] for the five [offerings]. On this maṇḍala, there is a golden plate (*svarṇapaṭṭa*) and so forth; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), silver, copper, and the like are indicated. The *saṃvarttikā* is an eight-petaled lotus. For the ninefold worship (*navārcana*), it is for the purpose of the worship of the Nine Lords (*naveśvara*). It is smeared with fragrance, moon, sun, and white substances, and anointed with rice (*śāli*). Fragrance (*gandha*) is musk (*kastūrikā*). Moon (*candra*) is sandalwood (*candana*). Sun (*arka*) is saffron (*kuṅkuma*). White lord (*śveteśa*) is camphor (*karpūra*).

*Aliḥ* means the cause. *Hemanālayā* means with a golden needle. *Alādhaḥ* means below the previously fashioned heavy circle (*gurumaṇḍala*). By the force of the context, the word "below" implies that one should fashion a circle measuring a fourth part [of the area] outside the four-finger width; that is, one should make a circle measuring a fourth part. For what purpose was it previously established? It was for the sake of installation (*sthāpanahetave*), meaning for the purpose of installing. Of what? Of the *nidāna*, the offering substance (*arghyadravya*) which brings about the presence of the Deity and is highly effective for invoking the presence of the worshipful sequential deities (*kramadevatā*). And it has been said:
That which bestows maturity upon the amorous words of young women, and which shakes off all trepidation during the act of love without obstacle.
"In that [place] where all the deities of the wheel-practice are gathered, it instantly produces that honeyed nectar (*mādhvīka*) wherein both worldly enjoyment and liberation reside.

Thus [it is said]. In the region of the primary *āla* (mouth/cavity), "mouth" refers to the fire (*agni*). On the southern side of the primary mandala, at a distance of four finger-breadths (*vedāṅgula*) from the exterior, and at a distance of four finger-breadths [from another point], with an extension of four finger-breadths...

The maṇḍala is four finger-breadths (caturaṅgula) in length, resembling a staff (daṇḍābha), for the purpose of worshipping the two gatekeepers during the worship of the two [deities]. That [space] is in the lunar portion (candrāṃśa) of that maṇḍala. In the northern direction, likewise, just as in the case of the gatekeeper maṇḍalas, they have a length and width of four finger-breadths (vedāṅgula) excluding the outer [area]. Thus is the syntactical connection: "the maṇḍala of the venerable gurus should be so. Regarding those who enjoy the [periods] beginning with Saṃvarta: *saṃvarta* means destruction (*kṣaya*).

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the two [other] times are indicated. These are the gurus of the respective ages (*yuga*). They are the participants in the delimitation of those respective times. From that measure, from the primary maṇḍala; "above," in the upper portion.

By the force of the word "above," [it refers to] the area four finger-breadths outside, because the divine guru-maṇḍala is to be made there afterwards. By the five previously mentioned verses, for the sacrificer at the seat of mantras as described in the primary [text].

For the purpose of worshipping the *mantrapīṭha*—the scripture composed by the Supreme Lord as the primary authority—one should perform the "sacrifice of the cause" (*hetuyajana*) at the conclusion of drawing the mandala, that is, at its completion. This sacrifice of the cause is performed for the deity established within the *arghya* mandala; one should begin the worship of that cause. The meaning is that one should perform it in order to purify the impurity residing in the abode of the bound soul (*paśu*).

In order to avoid the defect of dwelling in a site devoid of the *śivasaṃskāra* rites, and for the sake of immortality and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), he describes the procedure for the purification of the *arghya* water preceded by the purification of the maṇḍala with the three [mantras] beginning with *gana*. Therein, he states the five jewels: *gana*, *gagana*, and *svarga*. *Gana* is the elision of the initial syllable; *gagana* is the elision of the final letter; *svarga*—where *keśa* means the Lord of Waters (*jaleśa*).

The western portion is the lunar portion; Yama is the southern portion; the eastern is the front portion. This means that there are five jewels possessing their respective lusters. He states the seed-syllables of the five jewels, beginning with *śiva*: *śiva* is the letter *ga*; *Bhṛgu* is the letter *sa*; *Kāla* is the letter *ma*; *rakta* is the letter *pa*; *meṣa* is the letter *na*; *Dharā* is the letter *la*; and the sixth vowel is the letter *ū*. "Above that" means above that mandala. According to the tradition, just as those five jewels are placed in the mandala, so too are they [placed] in the *arghya* offering. *Glūṃ* for the Jewel of the Sky (*gaganaratna*); *glūm*.

*Slūṃ* for the jewel of heaven, *slūm*; *mlūṃ* for the jewel of the mortal world, *mlūm*; *plūṃ* for the jewel of the netherworld (*pātāla*), *plūm*; *nlūṃ* for the jewel of the serpents (*nāga*), *nlūm*. Then, following the five jewels and the treasure-trove (*nidhāna*), [one should worship] with the Goddess’s partless (*niṣkala*) ten-syllable mantra, and with the venerable new mantra of the New Lord (*Naveśvara*). By this [mantra], which is consecrated by the purification of mantras and which effects the destruction of all [impurities], because it has been purified by initiation, it removes all sins through sight, touch, and tasting. Regarding the son of Soma (the Moon), who is like Soma even in the Veda concerning the consumption of wine (*surā*), he is pure and non-dual. As it has been said:
"The Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice has liquor as its oblation; [there is] the reversal of the first two [days]," and so forth.
Therefore, for one who follows that path and possesses confidence in the words of Śiva—the supremely compassionate one who is the source of scripture—a pure cause is complete.

The meaning is that the sequential worship with an oblation consecrated by a specific mantra, performed by one who bestows the status of an "Ājñā-deha" (one whose body is the Command) upon all those who have attained perfection through the Command—such as Vyāsa, Vasiṣṭha, Saubhari, Viśvāmitra, Bharadvāja, and others—is the bestower of all accomplishments (*siddhi*).

The meaning of "one should satisfy the world" is that, through the propitiation of one’s own self as the Supreme Lord and the Supreme Deity consisting of consciousness (*cinmaya*), one should nourish the world composed of the thirty-six principles (*ṣaṭtriṃśattattva*), which is the manifestation of His own vibration (*spanda*).

This is the meaning of the passage beginning with "all limbs" and ending with "having sprinkled. The meaning is that the worshipper, with consecrated water, should first sprinkle all the limbs, all the implements of worship, all the mandalas, the seat of the mantra (*mantrapīṭha*), and the surrounding enclosures for the sake of purification. As it has been said:
Then, one should sprinkle with water consecrated by reciting the Śikhā-mantra the number of times prescribed in the *Śrītriṃśikā-śāstra*.
"Flowers and so forth, in sequence, [should be offered] to every liṅga or to the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila).
Thus [it is said]. Also in the *Śrītantrāloka*:
"Everything created [by impurity] is purified by the droplets of water from the arghya vessel."
"Through contact with the rays of the sun of Śiva, what other purification could there be?

Thus [it is said]. Regarding the *pāṇi-dehāsyanyāsas* (the placements on the hands, body, and mouth), which are the *karāṅgavaktranyāsas* (placements on the hands, limbs, and face) arising from the new Lord (*naveśa*), produced by the venerable Naveśvara—in the scripture of the determination of the venerable Śambhu—by this address to Aparṇā, the fitness of the audience is indicated. O you of great austerity! As it has been said by the great poets:
"Subsisting on the fallen leaves of trees herself, she has indeed reached the highest pinnacle of asceticism; moreover, even that was discarded by her.
Therefore, those conversant with ancient lore call her 'Aparṇā' (Leafless), O Priyamvadā.
Thus [ends the section on] the fivefold group, beginning with *svārājya*. "May you possess divine accomplishments," as before.
May there be auspiciousness!
Thus ends the first section in the *Śrīśambhunirṇayadīpikā*, composed by the venerable teacher Śivānandanātha, disciple of the venerable teacher Vidyānandanātha.
We perpetually praise that auspicious Śiva, the God who abides as the Self through the form of the sequence beginning with Śrī, Indu, Arka, Vahni, Śāstra, Ātman, Guru, and so forth.

“Dhātā,” and so forth. Dhātā is Brahmā; he “sūte,” meaning he creates. Having propitiated whom—having established that Supreme Śiva, who is one’s own self (*svātman*) and whose nature is consciousness (*cidrūpa*), through the recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) of Him as one’s own self—Brahmā performs his own function. The meaning is that Keśava and Rudra likewise perform their respective functions [having propitiated] the Supreme Śiva. Regarding the word “sūta”: this is its meaning. The Supreme Lord Himself, whose essence is Consciousness (*cidātman*), abiding in the form of the subjects such as the Creator (*sraṣṭṛ*), the Sustainer (*sthāpayitṛ*), the Destroyer (*saṃhartṛ*), and the Ordainer (*dhātṛ*), is indeed Brahmā.

"One's own self alone is the one Great Lord (*maheśvara*) of all living beings, expanded by the undivided awareness (*akhaṇḍāmarśa*) that 'I am this, whose form is the universe. Thus [it is said]. "Him, the Lord of All"—that is, the Supreme Subject, whose body is consciousness (*cidvapuṣ*), whose nature is the venerable Lord of Mantras (*mantrabhaṭṭāraka*). Listen! ... * * * * ... retain it! Therefore, [these are] the Śrī Maheśvara mantras and their adjuncts.

The connection is "by means of performance. The practitioner attains the five groups previously mentioned in the sūtra beginning with *svārājya*. The practitioner is one who is vigilant, performing the obligatory and occasional rites according to rule. He states the regulation regarding performance as "without women and so forth," which means he is free from: enjoyment of women at improper times, theft, dishonesty regarding wealth, longing for another's property, eating together with those initiated [into other systems], deceit, pride, envy, reviling those initiated, discord with the guru, living by crafts, and trickery. And on this point is the word of the Supreme Lord: that which is to be expressed is the attainment of the Self through immersion (*samāveśa*).
In the phrase "from practice" (*anuṣṭhānāt*), the *Śrīkramollāsa*, which contains the essence of devotion, is stated to be the means for attaining that [state].

143) By means of a *tatpuruṣa* compound in which the final member is predominant (*uttarapadapradhāna*)—namely, "the Supreme Lord" (*parameśvara*)—the fruit is described as the state of being the great sovereign of the wheel of consciousness characterized by absolute freedom (*svātantrya*), which does not look toward any other face.

As he will say: "He is the Blessed Lord himself," and "Śiva is twelvefold. The relationship between the subject matter (*abhidheya*) and the means (*upāya*)—namely, the state of being the goal and the means—is the connection;
thus, the subject matter, the means, the connection, and the purpose have been indicated. Now, he states the extraction of the nine lords with the words "eight":

"Eight" refers to those that will be mentioned hereafter as residing together, situated within a single manifestation. *Ambā* is the letter *ha*; *Bhṛgu* is the letter *sa*; *Kaṣa* is the letter *kṣa*; and *Yama* is the letter *ma*.

*Pūtalā* is the letter *la*. *Vajriṇī* is the letter *va*. *Pālī* is the letter *ya*. *Sarpo* is the letter *ra*. These letters are situated in the first and second positions. The change of gender is due to grammatical convention (*āgamika*). "The syllables" refers to the groups (*rāśi*). "The collection of syllables" has been stated. "Endowed with this" means endowed with these [syllables] which are about to be mentioned: "by *marmā*, *candra*, *aryamā*, and *agni*. *Marmā* is the vowel *ū*. *Candra* is the half-moon (*ardhacandra*).
*Aryamā*, denoting the sun, is the bindu (*bindu*). *Agni* is the *nāda*. It is the "giver of twelve parts," meaning it is the source of the manifestation of the universe (*viśvonmeṣa*).
This Lord Navīśvara has been extracted; He is Citīśa, Cinnātha, and Paramaśiva. Resembling the sun at its rising in the morning, He is the Peak (Kūṭa) whose essence is Śrīnivāsa.
[He is to be visualized] within the lotus of Svādhiṣṭhāna, the lotus of the self-abiding. As it has been said:

"From that Peak, which resembles a mass of lightning, one’s own Self arises in that form—the form of the illustrious Navīśvara. By means of a single breath-control (prāṇāyāma), until the cessation of the breath.

As long as there is breath, so long [one should apply] the *śrīnaveśvarakūṭa*. One should deposit it, that is, deposit it correctly, upon the limbs—that is, upon the body—by means of the appropriate yogas to be described hereafter, beginning with *ananta*. *Kūṭa* refers to the *kūṭa* under discussion. It is sixfold, meaning of six types; the sense is that one should understand them in their proper sequence. Regarding *ananta* and so forth: *ananta* is the letter *a*; *ākāra* is the form (*mūrti*); *trimūrti* is the letter *ī*; *marma* is the letter *ū*; and *bhautika* is the letter *ai*.

The Lord is the letter *au*; Sena and Mahāsena are the *visarga*. Like Bhīma and Bhāmā, these [letters] are joined with the celestial triad—the half-moon (*ardhacandra*), the point (*bindu*), and the sound (*nāda*)—beginning with *ha-sa-kṣa-ma-la-va-ya-rā-m*. He now describes the sequence of the ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*) starting with the word "the little finger" (*kaniṣṭhā*). The thumb is the "old" (*vṛddha*). The palm is the palate (*tālu*). Regarding the sequence of the ritual placement on the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*), he states the rule for the fingers with the word "thus" (*evam*). Thus, in this ritual placement on the hands, according to the procedure of the mantra, the heart is formed by the three middle fingers, the index finger, and the thumb.

The head is formed by two *ṛ* and *ta*, and the *ja* and *vṛddha* vowels; the tuft (*śikhā*) by one *vṛddha*; the armor (*kavaca*) by ten fingers each; the eyes (*netra*) by the ring, middle, and index fingers; and the weapon (*astra*) by the two thumbs and the thumbs of both hands. Regarding the body (*vigraha*): he states the sequence for the placement of the faces (*vaktra-nyāsa*) with the word "western" (*paścima*). The upward-facing face is the upper face, and the downward-facing face is the lower face. He states the sequence for the placement of the faces with the word "thief" (*cora*). By the word "thief," the cavity at the *trikā* location is meant.

The word *śruti* is connected with both the left and the right, namely the left *śruti* and the right *śruti*. By the word "mouth" (*mukha*), the location at the tip of the nose is indicated; by the word "hair" (*ka*), the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*) is meant; and by "crest" (*cūḍa*), the top of the head. Again, "the heap" (*rāśi*) means the heap behind. Having joined the single peak (*kūṭa*) and rendered it free from modification, there is the moon (*vidhu*) and the sun (*bradhna*). Fire is [indicated] by the term "cave" (*guha*). He describes the meditation on the moon as "white" (*sita*).

*Sitam* means white. *Abjam* means the moon (*jaivātṛka*). *Śaśāṅkastham* means situated upon the moon. *Goḍaḥ* means a skull. *Savyagam* means on the left side of the door. *Antarāyaḥ* means an obstacle (*vighna*). He states the mantra of the Moon with the words "of that" (*tasya*): "of that" refers to the Moon. *Īśvaraḥ* is the letter *ha*. *Ambu* is the letter *va*. *Sāvitrī* is the vowel *au*. By the syllables of Soma, Āryaman, and Kha—namely the digits (*kalā*), the bindu, and the nāda. The "atom" (*aṇu*) is placed at the beginning of the name; because it is given as the fourth [syllable] in the designation *Niśāṭana*, [the mantra becomes]: at the beginning and end of the name, the pair of seed-syllables (*bījayugmaka*) is *hvaṃ* and *hvaum*; thus: *Niśāṭanāya hvaum*.

In this system, one should recite five verses in both forward and reverse order at the beginning and end of all mantras. "The Sun is white... [and so forth]; the remainder is: "the light of day, the Sun, of red and non-red color, standing upon his mount, the horse."

*Apasavya* means situated on the right side of the door. *Ambara*... [with] mandalas, digits (*kalā*), points (*bindu*), and sounds (*nāda*). The mantra of that Lord of Days (*dinapati*) is *ambara*: *hrauṃ tamoraye hraum*. The mantra for the meditation on Fire (*agni-dhyāna-mantra*) is "yellow" (*pīta*); it is yellow in color. One should worship the harsh Fire with a ram as his vehicle. ... [the rest] is to be inferred. *Ambara* is the mantra. *Īśa* is the letter *ha*; *Saṃvarta* is the letter *kṣa*.

The Sāvitrī is the syllable *au*. The maṇḍala is as before; as at the beginning; like the mantra of the Moon. Regarding these two, the Sun and the Fire, this is the intended meaning: for the Sun and the Fire, there are two mantras [ending] with the dative case (*āyu*...); by means of enclosing the seed-syllable (*bīja*), it is "like the mantra of the Moon. *Ha kṣauṃ* is for Kālānala, *ha kṣauṃ*. *Ire*—*irā* is in the second half. *Irā* is the cause, not by name, but by implication through the ring finger joined with the thumb. And it has been said:

"Grasping the thumb in all [fingers]" means that the offering of the *bindu* (drop) is performed with the ring finger together with the thumb; this is the meaning. "Mudrā" refers to the *yonimudrā*; "strength" (*bala*) refers to the food offering (*naivedya*). By the preceding [verse], this is the meaning: preceded by the services of perfume, flowers, *dūrvā* grass, unbroken rice (*akṣata*), incense, lamps, mudrās, and food offerings, one should perform the offering of the *bindu* three times for each of the gatekeepers using the ring finger together with the thumb. Thus he describes the worship of the Mantra-Pedestal (*mantrapīṭha*) with the words beginning with "with verses" (*ślokaiḥ*). With five verses consisting of *praṇavas*, [one performs] the worship of the gatekeepers immediately following [the worship] on the Mantra-Pedestal in the book.

In the *Śrīmatapañcaka*, the *Śrīśambhunirṇaya*, and other such works, [the procedure] begins from the southern part of that scripture, according to the divisions ending with the gods (*surānta*) and the divisions ending with the deities (*devatānta*).

Within the fivefold division, there is that which is designated as "twelve finger-breadths" (*dvādaśāṅgula*) in the Mantra-pīṭha; it is located in the middle of the four parts, according to the sequence of entry and movement from south to north. Thus, the meaning is "by means of the fivefold division."

Such is the sequence of mantras: *aiṃ* to the mantra-deity, *aim*; *hrīṃ* to the mantra-deity, *hrīm*; *śrīṃ* to the mantra-deity, *śrīm*; *hsphreṃ* to the mantra-deity, *hsphrem*; *hsauṃ* to the mantra-deity, *hsaum*.
The connection is that one should then display the *yonimudrā* (the womb-gesture).

Having uttered the *navāmbara* mantra for the new garment in its long form—this is the meaning—one should offer three handfuls of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) along with the previously mentioned five mantras upon the seat of the mantra (*mantrapīṭha*), and then again with the heart-mantra (*hṛdayamantra*).

"One should display the *yonimudrā*. This means: after the worship of the Mantra-Pīṭha (*mantrapīṭhārcana*), by way of the distinction of "head-downwards" (*adhaśśirobheda*). That is, by the process of entry starting from the bottom and moving upwards. This is the traditional sequence (*sāmpradāyika*) here: *Āṃ* Ādigurunātha (*ām*). *Aṃ* Anādigurunātha (*am*). *Kuṃ* Kuleśvaragurunātha (*kum*). *Aṃ* Acintyagurunātha (*am*). *Mim* Mitragurunātha (*mim*). Having worshipped with these five mantras, according to the method of entry as in the Mantra-Pīṭha, using perfumes, flowers, and offerings, [one should worship] each one individually with the five [mantras].

One should offer incense, lamps, food offerings (*naivedya*), and so forth; this is the meaning expressed by the word "then" (*tataḥ*) and "the rest" (*śeṣa*). [The offering] is in the *medas*, which is the *svādhiṣṭhāna*.

Immediately following the worship of the five divine gurus, the connection is that one should form with both hands the *kamaṭhī* mudrā, which has the shape of a tortoise. Once [having done this], the garment is the ninefold peak-syllable (*navātmakūṭa*). What is its specific nature?

Its configuration is a single, staff-like form of light extending from the *svādhiṣṭhāna* up to the aperture of the head (*karandhra*). It is a corpse (*śava*), a ghost (*preta*), red in color (*rakta*) like a lotus (*kaja*) or water-born flower, with its head turned upward (*uttānamūrdhānam*) and its crown raised high.
“Holding a released *śakti*” means being liberated; *paraśakti* is a specific type of weapon, meaning one who holds an excellent *śakti*.

“A donkey” refers to fire (*agni*). “One should meditate on the corpse in the lotus of the *gurumaṇḍala*” is to be connected with what precedes it. He states the mantra for the worship of the fire in the form of a *preta* with the words beginning with “*amba*,” etc. “*Ambā*” is the letter *ha*.

*Ahiḥ* is the letter *ra*; *mūrttiḥ* is the vowel *ī*. *Hrīm* consists of the digits beginning with the moon (*candra*), along with the *bindu* and *nāda*. With this mantra, one should offer that [oblation] three times. Regarding the fire of that seat-fire: the lotus of the navel and head refers to the navel, the head, and the center of the navel; from that arises the lotus. Having meditated upon it thoroughly (*sandhyāya* = *samyak dhyātvā*), one should contemplate *aiṃ*, which is the *aikāra* belonging to the element of space (*bhautakhaṃ*). *Kha* refers to the half-moon and so forth. After meditating on the lotus arisen from the navel of the fire, the heart-intention is that one should contemplate a hexagon in the center of its pericarp. Having worshipped it thoroughly (*sampūjya* = *samyak pūjayitvā*), that seed-syllable of *Vāgbhava*—

"Perform worship"—by implication, one should understand that *vāgbhava* is indeed separate, or it should be construed with *tadaṇoḥ*. Both ways constitute our instruction. "The form arising from the crest (*cūḍā*) of that atom—that is, produced upon its head—one should meditate upon the form to be described hereafter"; this is connected with the verb contained in the phrase "one should meditate. In connection with the venerable Navātman, they state the bases for worship, beginning with "payodhara": the meaning of which is as follows.

It has been stated by Hīnāparameśvara that when worship is performed upon water, earth, fire, a book, a Śiva-liṅga, and a conscious being, each subsequent one yields a hundredfold greater fruit than the preceding one. Regarding these six locations, the *Śambara* states the materials for worship: "In water, [the worship] should be performed with *śambara* waters"—the word "worship" (*arcā*) is understood as the remainder of the sentence. Among the four Vedas, the supreme (*parā*) is the *Bṛhat*; [this applies] to the sun, a book, and the Śiva-liṅga.

With flowers and so forth—meaning with perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, and the like; at the end, within oneself, by means of the groups of women and so on, such as the enjoyment of women, the use of oils, and the eating of meat; and without [these external things], by means of the nectar of Kaja—the supreme nectar produced from the head—he states the rule regarding the time and occasion for the worship of those seeking liberation: "Pūjā" [means] at night, specifically at midnight, for those who sleep in the abode of the ancestors and the like; "the abode of the ancestors" refers to the cremation ground.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), secluded mountains and so forth are indicated. Because they are not within the sphere of ordinary people, they dwell there; the word "inferior ones" (*hināḥ*) is used, and the term "offering" (*argha*) is to be supplied as an ellipsis. For those dwelling in houses—namely, householders—it has been stated elsewhere that the time for the offering is during the night; here, it should be understood as being at midday. This is a type of sequential variation.
The remainder is as before; may there be auspiciousness.
Thus ends the second section in the *Śrīśambhunirṇayadīpikā* composed by the venerable teacher Śivānandanātha, disciple of the venerable teacher Vidyānandanātha. Śrī!
We praise that Śiva, who, though consisting of pure consciousness, always shines forth in nine ways through his sovereign freedom (*svātantrya*) in the form of all individual manifestations.

Regarding the words "atha" and so forth: *sāmrājya* means he who rules perfectly (*samyaṅ rājati*), namely the illustrious Navanātha; his *anubandhi* (concomitant) is *sāmrājya*. What is this world? It is the glory (*vaibhava*) of the ritual depositions (*nyāsa*), invocations (*āvāhana*), meditations (*dhyāna*), and so forth.

Terrifying to the gods who have undergone the shedding of karmic matter (*nirjaranirjarāṇāṃ devānām*), O Mother of all the gods (*sarvasurāmātaḥ*). [The word *mātaḥ*] is long according to the grammatical tradition (*āgamiko dīrghaḥ*). O Mother of all the gods (*sarveṣāṃ surāṇāṃ mātaḥ*).

From each single syllable of the secret code (*kūṭaikaikākṣarāt*)—from each one of the secret syllables—the limbs [of the mantra] are formed; even the three-limbed [mantra] is present on the two surfaces, that is, on the palms of both hands. The word "vṛddhā" is the name [of the goddess], and the term is connected with each [syllable]. The word "kaccha" (p. 149).

"Expressive of the palms and backs of the hands. This is the meaning: one should place the nine syllables beginning with *ha* and ending with *ḷ*, accompanied by *bindus*, upon the thumbs, forefingers, middle fingers, ring fingers, little fingers, and the backs of the fingers of both the right and left hands. "From the heart onwards" means starting from the heart. "Up to the armor" means ending with the *kavaca*. "The sword and the weapon. "The vital point (*marma*) is the letter *ū*. This is the meaning: with two syllables each, [one should assign them] from the heart up to the *kavaca*, using the letter *ū*.

"One should form the eye and the weapon with the *bindu*"; thus he describes the *daṇḍabhaṅginī* placement, beginning with "white" (*sita*) and so forth. "In the cavity" (*bile*) means in the *brahmarandhra*. "In the throat" (*gale*) means at the neck. "In the destruction" (*kṣaye*) means at the navel. "In all limbs" (*sarvāṅgake*) means from the *brahmabila* down to the ends of the feet. "From all limbs to the feet" (*sarvāṅgādi pādādi*) means from the feet up to the *brahmarandhra*. "From the foot to the cavity" (*padādrandhre*) means in the eight previously mentioned locations, starting from the feet and including the *brahmarandhra* and so forth; this is the meaning. For the sake of attaining stability of the body—that is, for the steadiness of the body. This is the sequence here: in the eight locations from the cavity to the end of the feet, one should place the eight syllables beginning with *ha* and ending with *ra*, preceded by the *bindu*, according to the syllables already mentioned.

Having performed the pervasive placement (*vyāpakanyāsa*) from the head to the feet again by means of the syllable *Ū* ending in the *bindu*, according to the method of breaking the staff (*daṇḍabhaṅginaya*), and having again performed the pervasive placement from the feet to the opening of the cave (*bilānta*) using the first letter of the new entry, one should perform the placement of the broken staff in reverse order across the eight locations from the feet to the opening of the cave during the remaining moment, as before.

He speaks again of the three limbs with the words "Then" (*tataḥ*). By means of the previously mentioned sūtra beginning with "Nan-ta," which bestows the body and grants longevity, [one attains] the supreme sound. Of the Paśyantī [speech], whose form is that of the venerable Sadāśiva—

Beyond the Creator, beyond the Progenitor Brahmā—by the two words "sound" (*śabda*) and "injunction" (*vidhi*), heaven and earth are indicated; by these two, the entire universe characterized by the elements and their derivatives is indicated. Beyond that universe is the God, the Great Sage, whose nature is that of the Supreme Subject (*parapramātṛ*). One should worship Him, Paramaśiva; this is the injunction. And it has been said:
"Those who, having abandoned the Lord who resides in the heart, go to another god..."
"They desire the jewel, even though the Kaustubha is clearly held in their hands.

150) Thus, having restrained the mind from its objects—having turned the mind away from the five objects such as sound—one should [meditate on] the white, the red, and the extremely red [forms] within the moon, sun, fire, and wind.

When the breath flows through the moon, sun, fire, wind, nose, or the vital air (*prāṇa*), one should contemplate this as his heart within the *cit* (the intellect) or the *hṛd* (the heart). When the breath of inhalation flows through the *iḍā*, one should contemplate a white-syllabled *kūṭa* (peak-syllable) in the throat; when it flows through the *piṅgalā*, a red-syllabled one in the heart; and when it flows through the *suṣumnā*, an intensely red one in the mouth. One should cause the *rāśi* (constellation/heap) to fall as the *kūṭa*. This is to be connected with the phrase "like the interior of a lotus. [She is] like a flame, possessing the color described, red in hue, with a body like the fiber of a lotus stalk. Because of its subtlety, the "third pair" is a qualification of the *kuṇḍalī*. By means of the *kuṇḍalī*, the venerable power of *Kuṇḍalinī*, who resides in the *mūlādhāra*.

"Raising up" (*utthāpana*) means the raising up of the *kūṭa*. By means of the cause consisting of the utterance of the venerable *Bhuvanaiśvarī*, within the lotus-bud which has become the seat by means of the fire arisen from the navel, [one performs it] in the interior of the venerable *Vāgbhava* seed-syllable, which is like the belly of a lotus.

"By the mere falling of that"—that is, by the mere falling of each respective *kūṭa*. "The form" (*mūrtiḥ*) refers to the form of the venerable Navaiśvara. "Through *mūrcchanā*"—by means of the mind being absorbed in that, through the contemplation of the dissolution (*laya*) of that *kūṭa*.

Through the dissolution into the peak of the form of light, the Self becomes the embodiment of the deity. By the analogy of molten gold becoming a solid mass, she removes the suffering—the worldly misery—of male practitioners (*sādhakas*). He describes the form to be meditated upon with the words beginning with "not fat" (*napīna*) and so forth: her complexion is like that of a fresh rain-cloud; her right foot has its big toe resting on a lotus, while the tip of the big toe of her left foot touches the fire-lotus at the navel; she is in the *argha-paryaṅka* posture, with the right leg extended.

Her right foot is extended across the region of the left hip. She possesses a great conch (*mahākaṃbu*), a great shell (*mahāśaṅkha*), and a jewel-wheel (*ratnacakra*). A great serpent, such as Vāsuki, with a crest-jewel upon its head, is coiled around her. She wears a lotus-skin and a tiger-skin. Her hips are adorned with a *kaṭṭārī*—a specific type of weapon known by that name—and she is endowed with a girdle of lightning-bands. She is decorated with a human skull and adorned with a garland of human skulls and severed arms.

She has five faces and five mouths; she has fifteen eyes and five eyes. She is the element of Brahmā. With her right hands—the non-left (apasavya) arms—she holds weapons and implements for the sake of the liberation of the world and for the sake of the liberation of the practitioner. [She holds] the foot of Brahmā, a fragrant Pāribhadra flower, a fragrant flower from the Kalpa-tree, a rosary for recitation, and a book.

The ellipsis implies that she holds the mudrā of fearlessness (*abhayamudrā*) which destroys fear with her right hands. Her face is always smiling; "toward the gods" means her face is always smiling toward the *lekhās*, the gods. Regarding the term *śmaśānaka-śmaśayana*: by the elision of the letter *ya* and the application of the rule for lengthening similar vowels (*savarṇadīrgha*), *śmaśānaka* becomes *śmaśāna*. *Śmaśayana* refers to lying in a *śmaśāna* (cremation ground); the meaning is "lying in fire. She is always surrounded by multitudes of spirits (*paretas*) who take the forms of both the moving and the unmoving (*acarācara*).
He plays equally with one who is a skull-bearer consisting of pure consciousness.
I bow to the Lord, the sovereign of the three worlds, white with ashes, three-eyed, bearing the trident,
having a serpent as his sacred thread, and crowned with a digit of the moon.
"I bow to [the deity] whose lower garment is white with the halo of the silken cloth streaming from his own body, and who is adorned for the festival of dance by a shimmering garland of skulls.

Passages such as these are to be examined here. Regarding the phrase "of the sacrificer" (*yajataḥ*), meaning of the practitioner (*sādhaka*) performing the sacrifice (*yajana*), starting from the worship of the trident (*śūlapūjā*): this is its meaning.

To whatever extent there is illusion arising from the three worlds, to that same extent it proceeds from the propitiation of the wheel (*cakra*). Furthermore, one who is devoted to the worship of the wheel becomes capable of displaying illusions, such as those of Śambara and others.

From the worship of the banner (*dhvaja*)—that is, from the veneration of the banner—there comes the going to the fourteen levels of the worlds, the reaching of the fourteen planes of existence, the attainment of knowledge of all times, and the accomplishment of knowing the three times at all times.

From the worship with fragrant flowers, one always obtains the state of being fragrant and the worship of the flowers of the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*) that never wither. From the fruit of the recitation and worship, there is mastery over hundreds of earths, universal sovereignty, and the complete accomplishment of all mantras. There is the fulfillment of all mantras through auspicious sounds, and the attainment of all success from the fruit of the rosary used for recitation. Regarding the six destinies—the six states of gods, humans, ancestors, *asuras*, *rākṣasas*, and *piśācas*—there is the destruction of obstacles above, the destruction of obstacles within the cosmic egg starting from the intermediate space (*antarikṣaloka*), and the destruction of obstacles below—that is, the destruction of obstacles moving toward the lower realms.

This is the mantra for the worship of the *astra* (weapon), which destroys obstacles within the cosmic egg (*aṇḍa*) starting from the *bhūrloka*. He states the mantras beginning with "Ambā" and so forth: *Ambā* is the letter *ha*; *krūra* is the nasal dot (*bindu*). The tenth [letter] is the *bindu* itself.

This is the sequence of the mantra: *Haṃ* to Brahmahara—*haṃ*. *Saṃ* to the trident (*triśūla*)—*saṃ*. *Kṣaṃ* to the discus (*cakra*)—*kṣaṃ*. *Maṃ* to the banner (*dhvaja*)—*maṃ*. *Laṃ* to the supreme (*para*)—*laṃ*. *Vaṃ* to the giver of Brahman (*brahmada*)—*vaṃ*. *Yaṃ* to the flower of the *pāribhadra* tree—*yaṃ*. *Raṃ* to the rosary for recitation (*jāpyamālā*)—*raṃ*. *Ūṃ* to the book (*pustaka*)—*ūṃ*. *Aṃ* to the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*)—*aṃ*. Thus it is said.

Now he describes the worship of the New Lord (Naveśa)—beginning with the word "evam" (*thus*). Having recited the root mantra and the peak-syllable (kūṭa) of the New Lord, and having established the vital breaths—that is, having restrained the flow of the prāṇas—one should worship.

The "arghya vessel" is the vessel for worship. "Datteram" means another vessel filled with *irā* (the offering substance) has been given. By the word "ca" (*and*), the phrase "having given these" is conjoined. One should worship the New Lord (Naveśvara) by means of the pure cause—the previously established and consecrated cause; this must be supplied to complete the sense. This is for the purpose of worshipping these seed-mantras; [this occurs] between those two.

The connection is as follows: *gandha* refers to sandalwood (*candana*) and *kīra* (saffron), which are smeared with white sugar (*sitayā śarkarayā*) and *gandhakīra*; *miśrīkṛtam* means mixed with those two; thus one should demonstrate the water and so forth.

There are five kinds of food offerings (*naivedya*). "Edibles" refers to fruits. "White *dūrvā*" refers to white *dūrvā* grass. The syntactical construction is: "one should offer [these] upon the head. Regarding "the subtle (*aṇuka*) threefold [mantra]," *aṇu* refers to the nine-syllable peak mantra (*naveśakūṭa*).

While recollecting the nine-syllable mantra three times, one should display the *yonimudrā* three times. For the sake of the world's affairs—that is, for the welfare of the world—the "vital breaths" (*prāṇāḥ*) are the life-force of this deity.

By this, there may be Bhairavas who are powers (*śakti-bhairavāḥ*), and there may be Bhairavas who possess power (*śaktimantaḥ*). The remainder [of the sense] is that "there are eight. I speak; that is, I indicate. The meaning is that I shall reveal [them] through the sequence of explicit instruction.
O Śaktināyikā, you who are the principal among all powers. O Śakti! This is the vocative. May there be auspiciousness.
Thus ends the third section in the *Śrīśambhunirṇayadīpikā*, composed by the venerable teacher Śivānandanātha, disciple of the venerable teacher Vidyānandanātha. Salutations!
That which is the embodiment of the six female messengers (*dūtī*) through their state as limbs of dissolution (*laya*) and enjoyment (*bhoga*).
We praise that Śiva, who is ever awake for the protection of all. Regarding the phrase *sanidāna* and so forth:

*sanidānam* means accompanied by the primordial cause, the New Lord (*naveśvara*). The word *surāḥ* is used in the sense of the genitive; it connects with what follows as "the means (*sādhana*) of the gods. The meaning is:

together with the root cause, there is the means for the gods—the life-breaths of the New Lord. The *surās* are the sequential deities (*kramadevatās*), the causes that serve as the basis for the accomplishment of the universe. [The term *janasiddhyai*] means for the sake of human success, that is, for success in this world.

This [word] is used in the sense of the third case (*tṛtīyārthe*). By practitioners, as the sole means for the sake of the gods—that is, as the exclusive means related to the causes of the gods—the "means" (*sādhana*) consists in the securing of ownership for the deities.

"In sequence" (*kramāt*) means according to the order of worship, recitation, and so forth. "O Śakti! is an address. Simultaneously, that is, all at once, having first worshipped the deity in the pericarp of the *guru-maṇḍala* lotus, one should [worship] subsequently on the eight petals starting from the east.

The purport of this much of the text is that one should worship the eight pairs beginning with Rūpa and Maṇḍala. Therefore, because it is not [to be done] simultaneously, for that reason it is stated [to be performed] through rites such as sequential worship, meditation, and recitation (*japa*), as well as by means of the deities of sequential worship, meditation, the recitation of hymns, recitation, fire-offerings (*homa*), and so forth. In the neuter position, starting from the eastern direction and ending with Mṛḍa, up to the region of the northeast (*īśadigbhāga*).

The skull is half-mutilated; the hands rest upon the breasts and the chin, and the chin rests upon the hands. It is blood-like, red in color. In the lap of these Bhairavas, beginning with Maṅgala, one should place Ghoṇikā, Vārāhī, Śāṅkī, and Indrāṇī. One should [place] the eight syllables beginning with *ha* and ending with *ra*, each distinct by means of the seed-syllable *bindu*, differentiated according to their respective seed-natures.

"Distinct" means impermanent. "Joined with the ninth" means joined with the ninth vowel; "with their own anusvāras" means accompanied by the nasal dot (*bindu*). By these—namely, the *kūṭa-mantras* such as *hūṃ* and so forth, which are conjoined with the secret power (*guhya-śakti*) and the three forms (*trimūrti*), consisting of the syllables *hīṃ* and so on—at the end of this, that is, at the conclusion of the worship of the eight couples (*mithuna-aṣṭaka*). The word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "incense etc. indicates lamps and other such offerings.

Furthermore, after the sequential worship, there is the playing of musical instruments such as the *ḍhakkā*, *maddala*, and *bherī*. This is the procedure here: one should worship the eight pairs beginning with Maṅgalā, who are red in color and have their hands placed upon the breasts of their consorts, whose hands hold a skull-cup (*kapāla*) and a trident (*śūla*), and who are mounted upon their own [consorts'] bodies. This is the sequence here:
*HŪṂ maṅgalamahābhairavānandanātha HŪM | HĪṂ brahmāṇī parā abba HĪM*.

SŪṂ Carcaka-Mahābhairavānandanātha SŪM | SĪṂ Māheśvarī Parā Abba SĪM | KṢŪṂ Yogamahābhairavānandanātha KṢŪM | KṢĪṂ Kaumārī Parā Abba KṢĪM | MŪṂ Harasiddha-Mahābhairavānandanātha MŪM | MĪṂ Vaiṣṇavī Parā Abba MĪM |
LŪṂ Bhaṭṭa Mahābhairavānandanātha LŪM. LĪṂ Vārāhī Parā Abbā LĪM. (p. 155) PŪṂ Kilikila Mahābhairavānandanātha PŪM. PĪṂ Indrāṇī Parā Abbā PĪM.
"Yūṃ Kālarātra-mahābhairavānandanātha Yūm; Yīṃ Cāmuṇḍā Parā Abbā Yīm;

Rūṃ Bhīṣaṇa-mahābhairavānandanātha Rūm; Rīṃ Mahālakṣmī Parā Abbā Rīm. Thus it is said. In the manner described, one should worship the heart and the other limbs with the six *rasas* (flavors) in the nine [locations]. This means that in the form of the illustrious Nine Lords (*navaiśvaramūrti*), one should perform the worship of the limbs of dissolution (*layāṅga*).

Having made the request and having fully informed [the deity] of the subsequent rites—namely, the worship of the limbs of enjoyment (*bhogaṅga*) and the worship of the enclosure of the womb (*garbhāvaraṇa*)—he states the locations with the words "jātā" and so forth. In *jātavedasi* (the southeast), in *bhūteśe* (the northeast), in *yātudhāne* (the southwest), and so on. "Nine-headed" (*navamauli*) refers to the assembly of gods (*devavrāta*), a multitude of deities, near the place of sacrifice. "By reason" (*kāraṇena*) means by cause; the heart of the matter is that the propitiation of deities must not be performed without a cause. Just as in the Soma sacrifice one does not worship Indra and the others without Soma, [here too] it refers to the mudrā named "Yoni" (*yonināmikā*). This is the remainder [of the sense].

*Jāpyaṃ* refers to the recitation (*japa*). *Naveśvarī* is an address of invocation. Regarding the phrase "of the heart and so forth" (*hṛdādīnām*): its meaning is that the recitation should be performed by assigning ten [repetitions] to each of the limbs, beginning with the heart (*hṛdaya*).
He states the hymn of praise (*stotra*), beginning with "namaḥ" and so on; the word "namaḥ" is connected with the dative case ending. *Druhiṇa* is Brahmā; *Vaikuṇṭha* is Viṣṇu.

The power (*śakti*) of those two consists of the power of creation (*sṛṣṭi*) and the power of maintenance (*sthiti*), and their progenitor (*prasūti*) is Śiva, whose nature (*dharma*) is the source of their birth—to him [be salutation]. *Ādhāra* is the *mūlādhāra*.

Sādhī is the *svādhiṣṭhāna* at the navel; *daṃśa* is the *kanda* location at the heart; *kaṇṭha* is the throat; *bindu* is the *ājñā* location; *bila* is the *brahmabila*; the *ṣoḍaśānta* is the ground of emission (*visarga*); and the *racyanta* is the ground of the *dvādaśānta*. To the one who rains down the movement and non-movement within those nine supports (*navādhāra*), whose body performs coming and going—[for such a one] there is birth after birth as experience, the enjoyment of karma;

dissolution is death; the past is *bhūta*; the present is *varta*; and that which is called the future is *bhaviṣyat*. To the knower of the discourse on knowledge, the one who knows the continuity of knowledge regarding that world—it has been said:
For the person who is unborn within the realms of existence, there is the past, the present, and the future; indeed,
with an unobstructed eye consisting of gnosis, he perceives this triad.

Thus [it is said]. The six waves are hunger, thirst, sorrow, delusion, old age, and death. To the destroyer of the proponents of non-existence (*asattāvādin*) and emptiness (*śūnyavādin*); that is, to the one who destroys those who maintain that things are non-existent or empty. As it has been said: "Let alone existence itself, which does not exist without Your power;
for those whose discourse on Your refutation is not possible without You."

Thus are the six destinies: gods, humans, ancestors, *suras*, *rakṣasas*, and *piśācas*. Repetition is the intensive expression of an action (*kriyāsamabhihāra*). To the one who causes the destruction of decay and existence—to the one who effects the destruction of both decay and existence—to the agent of the destruction of decay and existence. As it has been said:
"O Lord, that which is existent is necessarily the supreme non-existent, and that which is existent is beyond that."
"And you, being other than both the non-existent and the existent, are therefore composed of both existence and non-existence.

[Thus it is said. To the giver of immortality, the bestower of liberation (*mokṣa*). "Born from five verses" means produced by five lotuses. "The Lord of Men" refers to the supreme practitioner (*sādhaka*). "For the completion of worship" means for the sake of one who has properly propitiated [the deity]. "For the attainment of all *anu*siddhis" means for the attainment of all mantras. "For liberation" means for *mokṣa*. "For happiness" means for enjoyment. "Homa" refers to the oblation related to the New Lord (*naveśvara*). [This is] for the attainment of the three commands (*ājñā*).

For the sake of accomplishing the three commands (*ājñātraya*). The three commands are as before, at the conclusion of the worship, hymn, and recitation (*japa*). One should worship the New Lord (*naveśvara*) with an oblation (*homa*)—this is the meaning. The worship of the messenger (*dūtī*) is the worship of the deities of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅgadevatā*).
In the *Bhavya* [tantra], it is said "having been invited. May there be auspiciousness!
Thus ends the fourth section in the *Śrīśambhunirṇayadīpikā*, composed by the venerable teacher Śivānandanātha, disciple of the venerable teacher Vidyānandanātha.
Prosperity belongs to him who constantly abides in the one possessing the crest-tuft through worship, oblations, and ritual observances.
"He always bestows fruit upon the priest; let us praise that auspicious one.

Regarding the passage beginning with "Vahni" (Fire): this is the meaning. This fire which shines externally is not distinct from the Self of Śambhu, because its very nature is a mass of light. And it has been said: "This Agni is indeed Rudra. Furthermore, he states that this form of fire is twofold: internal and external. The internal is the *bindu*-fire (*baindavāgni*).

"Having churned" means having performed the act of churning. "Contained within the wood" means contained within the fuel-wood. "As obtained" means as established. "Dhanañjayayogin"—the word "he" (*saḥ*) is to be supplied [as the subject].

"That fire"—make it equal by means of one's own *vaidava* [fire], that is, by the light of the *bindu* situated in the station of the Command (*ājñā*). "That [is] the *khara*"—this is the connection with what follows. In a four-cornered (*vedāśra*) square measuring seventeen finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), or in a space of seventeen finger-breadths, [there should be] a single thorn (*kaṇṭaka*). One should dig so that the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) has a thorn of one finger-breadth.

The meaning is as follows: for a circular [pit] with a girdle (*mekhalā*) of six finger-breadths (*rasāṅgula*) and a yoni of twelve finger-breadths, [the measurements are] six finger-breadths and twelve finger-breadths; and for a yoni of twelve finger-breadths with a girdle of six finger-breadths, they are likewise six and twelve. "Khara" means fire. He states the alternative for the pit (*kuṇḍa*): "Or else. In such a case—meaning in a circular shape endowed with the previously mentioned characteristics—one should [pour] milk (*kṣīra*), that is, fresh milk, or the essence of milk which is clarified butter (*ghṛta*), or white sugar (*sitā-śarkarā*). This is intended to exclude the previously mentioned [other substances like] milk and so forth. It should be measured at the size of a cat's paw (*bilālapada-sammita*), that is, the dimension of a cat's foot.

The meaning is that one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) after having meditated upon the formless [deity] with the fire accompanied by meditation on the formed [deity]. Regarding the "heart and so forth," this refers to the heart and other limbs; even in the case of the "constant practice" (*nityānuṣṭhāna*), for the sake of attaining mastery over the mantra, an oblation of one-tenth the quantity of the root-mantra oblation must be performed. As for the "mudrā," it is the *yonimudrā*; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), [other mudrās are implied].

The lamp is observed. *Laya* is the withdrawal of the fire. Three times means three repetitions within the circle of the bow (*kodaṇḍamaṇḍala*), at the location of the *bindu*. [This is done] because of the application of the forehead mark (*tilaka*) upon the weapon (*astra*). *Visarjana* is the dismissal. *Naveśvara-homa* is not a sacrifice; rather, it is a sacrifice related to the New Lord (*naveśvara*). May there be auspiciousness! Thus ends the fifth section in the *Śrīśambhunirṇayadīpikā*, composed by the venerable teacher Śivānandanātha, disciple of the venerable teacher Vidyānandanātha.
O Śrī,
we praise that Śiva, the foremost physician who destroys whatever disease arises and who is the enemy of the mass of ailments.

"Homādityādi" [means]: for the Guru, for the sake of the Guru. "In front of the Lord" means in the presence of the honored new master. "Afterwards" means subsequently. "For the destruction of one's own sins" means for the purpose of destroying one's own previously accumulated evil. "In that very manner, one should perform the practice numbering one hundred thousand"—that is, one should attend to it; the meaning is that one should recite it. "Before" means previously. "Diseases" refers to those existing in the body; the connection is with "fevers and so forth. "Bestowing a body" means bestowing health upon one's own body. This is an adjective qualifying the recitation (*japa*), [specifying] that it is accompanied by fire-offerings (*homa*).

"The word of Śrīśambhu" means that this too is the speech of the venerable Śambhu. Regarding the term "phlegm" (*śleṣma*): here, for the sake of syntactic unity, the words *yat* and *tat* are to be supplied;

thus, the series of fevers arising from the three humors (*doṣa*) taken two at a time, such as cold and heat, constitutes the category of fever. "Ayutaṃ naveśam": these are two separate words. The meaning is: having recited the *naveśa* ten thousand times. (p. 159)

"One should perform a hundred *homa*s" means one should offer a hundred oblations (*āhuti*s). Here, the word "hundred" signifies a thousand. "White mustard seeds" refers to *siddhārtha*. "A hundred handfuls"—meaning a hundred handfuls of those difficult to sever—is an adjective qualifying all types of fever. "Delusion" means falsehood. Therefore, in this context, it means that [the fever] becomes false. "With great labored breaths" means with upward gasps, having reached the state of exhaustion or departure [from life]. "Near death" means untimely death. "Rendered useless" means made wretched. The word "as if having seen" is to be supplied [to complete the sense]. The ellipsis is that "auspiciousness" or "happiness" results.

"Vikāram" means a morbid transformation. "Arśasaḥ" refers to hemorrhoids (durmāṃsa). "Gaudasya" means difficult to conquer, i.e., impossible to overcome. "Atra" means in this disease, which serves as the cause. "Pañcavidham gulmam" [is used] in the sense of the third case (instrumental), as seen in the use of the word "ṣaḍ". Alternatively, there is a fivefold division according to the difference in location, as it has been said:
"Because of its being condensed, even though it is formless, it is regarded as having taken on a form."
"Gulma" is said to be that which resides in the bladder, the navel, the heart, and the flanks.

By implication, "three thousand" [is meant]. "Inextricable" (anistāram) means impossible to cross over. Of the black antelope (kṛṣṇasāra), belonging to the black pond (kṛṣṇakuṇḍa). "Kravya" means flesh.

"Afflicted by the disease of stones" (aśmarīrasita) means seized by the ailment of urinary calculi. By implication, "five thousand rose-apples" (jambūphala). "Vomiting" (chardim) refers to the spitting up of food; "difficult to conquer" (durjaya) and "constantly adhering" (nityānuṣakta). "Pala" means meat. And for the destruction of bodily diseases.

For the destruction of diseases residing firmly within the body, one should offer as an oblation (*homayet*) a large, spreading leprosy (*mahāśvitra*)—a form of *kuṣṭha* characterized by various colors such as red, black, and white—along with *udumbara* fruits. By implication, "ten thousand" (*ayuta*) is understood [as the number of offerings]. Here, the triad consisting of Soma, Aryaman, and Khara is indicated. With the dust of Soma, Aryaman, and Khara, the meaning of the sentence is that one should recite [the mantra] three hundred thousand times.

Regarding the specific types of grains: "The *kalāya*, *udhānya*, and *asitaśūka* are synonyms for barley (*yava*); the *koka* is the green variety; and that which is *satīnaka*... so says Amarasimha. By implication, "ten thousand" (*ayuta*) refers to ten thousand handfuls (*muṣṭi*), and "thirty thousand" (*tryayuta*) refers to thirty thousand handfuls. *Udaranāyaka* means one with a large belly (*mahodara*). "Ten thousand blades of *dūrvā*" (*dūrvāyuta*) means ten thousand *dūrvā* grasses. With the seeds increasing—[that] great calamity.

*Unmāda* is the delusion of the mind. It belongs to *raktavedhas*, the *brahmavr̥kṣa*. — By the power of the prescribed *homa* for that, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times (*lakṣa*); this is to be inferred. Having first performed the recitation (*sañjapya*), by means of the omission of the drop (*bindu*). These are two words. Having first properly recited [it], for the sake of the pervasive body of the Self, of the one who has entered the new [state]—this is the meaning of "one by one" (*ekaikaśaḥ*). There are ten million varieties (*koṭibheda*) for each of the great diseases. For the purpose of destroying them, one should first recite the hundred thousand [mantras] of the New Lord (*naveśvara*). Furthermore, as before, one should offer oblations (*juhuyāt*) with the juice of the forest *sūraṇa* tuber.

Pure and healthy—meaning one whose faculties are sharp. "Sanā" means eternally. Regarding "sanā," Amarasimha states: "The word *sanā* is used in the sense of 'eternal' or 'external'. "Nāvaka" refers to that which pertains to the New Lord (the youthful Maheśvara). "The sole causes for the newness of the body" means for the sake of attaining a fresh state of the body; that is to say, for the destruction of wrinkles and grey hair. Having meditated upon the Enemy of the multitude of diseases, who is untainted by time—the Great Lord who is the adversary of the entire mass of ailments—may there be auspiciousness.
Thus ends the sixth section in the *Śambhunirṇayadīpikā*, composed by the venerable teacher Śivānandanātha, disciple of the venerable teacher Vidyānandanātha.
Śrī! He whose self is the seed of the nine primordial natures (*prakṛti*), whose body consists of nine syllables, and who is ninefold—*Śrīḥ*.
We praise that Śiva, whose essence is the noble and supreme Lord of the Immortals, who shines forth.

[Regarding the verse beginning with] "the group of nine" (*navakam*), etc.: the sequence is "the group of five" (*pañcakam*) and "the group of nine. The fifth is the seed-syllable of the Earth (*bhū-bīja*). It has the luster of a palm tree, meaning it is like yellow orpiment (*haritāla*), situated in the abode of gold at the *mūlādhāra*. It is "with a dot," meaning accompanied by the nasal bindu.

The "abiding until the end of life" means until the end of the duration of the breath, as long as it lasts in its entirety. In the *mūlādhāra*, which is golden in color, one should meditate on the form of the seed-syllable of Earth (*bhū-bīja*), which is the color of yellow orpiment, accompanied by the nasal drop (*bindu*) and the crescent moon (*naveśa*).

The meaning of the sentence is that one whose vital breath is restrained should meditate thus. Within half a year—that is, six months—the Lord of Yogis (*yogīśvara*), the supreme among practitioners, [attains] *bali*... [and so forth].

"From the year" (*abda-taḥ*) means from the [lunar] year; this is the ellipsis. "Heaviness" (*gurutām*) means density. "Bestowing the attainment of Indra’s intelligence, splendor, strength, and luster" (*śakramati-bhā-balatā-āpti-dām*) means bestowing the attainment of Indra’s earth, intellect, splendor, power, and radiance. "After three years endowed with qualities" (*guṇavatsarataḥ trivatsarāt*). "Vajra-body" (*vajra-kāyaḥ*) means a body as firm as a thunderbolt. "Lord of the earth" (*dharādhipaḥ*) means a sovereign of the world. "By twelve years" (*ravi-saṅkhyaiḥ*) means by twelve years. "Equal to Śatakratu" (*śatakratu-tulyaḥ*) means equal to Indra. "Below that, in the order of extraction" (*tad-adha uddhāra-krame*) refers to its [subsequent] sequence.

The construction is: "the word situated below the letter *la*. [The word] is *kṣatra*, which means at the navel (*abhau*). *Himānī* is a mass of snow; its lord is the moon (*candra*); its *alaṃ* is its orb (*maṇḍala*). "Situated therein" means situated within the lunar orb. The "word" (*pada*) is the letter *pa*. *Gada* is disease. "From Ravi" means from the twelfth year. "In Vidhi" means in the world of the moon (*candraloka*). It is the eighth [letter] from the ninth *va* of Śambhu (i.e., *śa*). [It is] in *svādhāra*.

In the Svādhiṣṭhāna maṇḍala, [the letter] together with Rudra and the bindu, according to the aforementioned time—that is, by the sequence of time stated in the previous sūtra—in the city of Dhanañjaya, in the world of fire (Agniloka), the seventh from the two horses (dvājin) and the self (ātman), which is the first of the primary [vowels];

the first of the nine lords (naveśa); for the sake of purification; for the sake of complete purity; the twelve-year [cycle] (ravihāyana); in the cave (bila); in the station of the Command (ājñāsthāna); the pair of Śambhu, which is the second of the nine lords; having the color of the risen sun, red, and residing in the letter A.

"Endowed with the bindu" means [the letter] in the city of Parā, in the city of Śakti, on the boat in the state of Vaibhava. "The pervasive fourth" means the pervasive fourth; it is adorned by that very fourth, meaning it is embellished, having the bindu as its head.
That third is the third of the Lord of the New.
In the eternal abode, in the middle of the bow, Rudra is the Bindu (the point). Having become omniscient, one attains lordship over all worlds and their lords; from truth, truth [is attained].

In the fat, in the Svādhiṣṭhāna [cakra], she who resembles the sun is red in color. Kṛti means Prakṛti. Her ninth [form] belongs to the Lord of the New (Navīśa); this refers to the ninth [digit]. He describes the meditation on the half-moon and the Bindu with the words "kārmuka" and so forth.

In the form of the bow’s disk... the syllable *śa* belongs to the maker of the sheath (*kośakāra*). In the six-cornered [figure], the word *kuśa* appears in the form of the Pārijāta tree; the word *kuśa* is a part of the word *ku*. The syllable *pa*... [is the remainder].
"A portion of a flower" means that, by that [portion], there is the white color in the appearance of the flower. The mandalas are characterized by the half-moon, the bindu, and the petals.

"Situated within them" means situated within the three mandalas. "Vibhvī" means possessing great majesty (*mahāvibhūti*). "Kuṇḍalī" means the Kuṇḍalinī power (*śakti*) raised up by a new impulse. "Dwelling in the aperture" means residing in the station of the Brahma-aperture (*brahmarandhra*).

One should meditate on [the goddess] situated above the three maṇḍalas of the white, solar, and red [lights], which are respectively characterized by a white half-moon, a sun, and a bindu; and above the three maṇḍalas of nāda, which are characterized by a white [half-moon], a sun, and a red [bindu]. Furthermore, one should meditate on Indupānī, who is characterized by the moon and whose form is that of drinking, streaming forth a stream of nectar—this is the remainder [of the instruction]. During the two-month period [of meditation], she is thus as described, her speech unerring. By the word "skhalita" (errant), the mere departure [of the speech] is indicated. By the word "manaḥ" (mind), the sense is that she speaks the desired meaning through the mere non-departure of the mind from its source. And it has been said:

"For what one meditates upon with the mind, that one speaks with speech"; and also, "The mind is the precursor, speech is the follower. Regarding the word *sarva* (all) and so forth: the word *sarva* is connected to the four categories beginning with the scriptures (*śāstra*).

The terms *āgama* and *āmnāya* have been explained right here. It has as its subject matter all the authoritative scriptures (*adhikāgama*). This [text] addressed to Śiva partakes of the qualities of Śambhu; it is the glorious majesty (*vaibhava*) established in attributes such as omniscience, belonging to the illustrious Śambhu—may there be auspiciousness!
Thus ends the seventh section in the *Śrīśambhunirṇayadīpikā*, composed by the venerable teacher Śivānandanātha, disciple of the venerable teacher Vidyānandanātha. Śrī.

We praise that Śiva, who, through various specific meditations, possesses various manifestations of glory and is the eternal bestower of their respective fruits. Following the meditation on his glory (*vaibhava*), the meditation on Śakti is now described. Regarding the phrase "the Śākta," etc.: the connection is that it is the meditation related to Śakti. It bestows many diverse supernatural accomplishments (*siddhis*).

She is the bestower of many diverse accomplishments (*siddhis*), the giver of immortality, the one who grants the state of being immortal; that is, she possesses the quality of being a bestower of accomplishments in such a manner. Furthermore, she is the giver of other knowledges—meaning she bestows the knowledge of the past, future, and present. And she says that this very power (*śakti*) manifests in this way: "the body (*piṇḍa*)," etc., ending with "satisfaction. By the word "etc.," the senses, mind, intellect, and so forth are indicated. Thus, she is the one who leads to the satisfaction of the body and the rest. She is the power inherent within the mantras.

[She is] situated in the middle of that wheel of letters (*varṇacakra*), meaning she resides in the center of the wheel of letters contained within the mantra. Again, he describes the manifestation (*vibhūti*) of Śakti with the words beginning "firm" (*dṛḍha*). Here, the sixfold [set] of fruits is said to be firmness. "Beauty" (*lāvaṇya*) refers to the beauty of the body. "Command" (*ājñā*) refers to the attainment of the power of command (*ājñāsiddhi*). By the word "atom" (*aṇu*), the attainment of the power of mantra (*mantrasiddhi*) is meant. By the word "omniscient" (*sarvajña*), the attainment of omniscience (*sarvajñatvasiddhi*) is meant. (p. 164)

By the word *amṛta* (nectar), *kaivalya* (liberation) is meant. [The syllable] *śakti* has the form of the *śakti-mantra*. *Khara* is the letter *repha* (*r*). It is the movement (*sañcāra*). Because it is dominated by *prāṇa* in the morning, it indicates the letter *ha*. *Śakti* is the vowel *ī*. *Indu* is the half-moon, the dot (*bindu*), the *anusvāra*. "Born from *nāda*" means produced from *nāda*. The meaning is that *śakti* is born from *repha*, *ha*, *māyā*, *indu*, *bindu*, and *nāda*. Thus, *rahīm*. He states the location for the movement of *śakti*: "hem" and so forth. The word *hema* denotes the *mūlādhāra*. By the word *abja* (lotus), which denotes the moon, the location of the navel is indicated. By the word *sādhi*...

*Śvādhiṣṭhāna* is the *bila*, and the place of *ājñā* is *Āravatī*; the meaning is that [the mantra] has the nature of moving through the six *ādhāras*. It is consecrated by the mantra beginning with "in Śiva," and so forth. Regarding "the self" (*ātman*) and so on: this is the meaning.

The sequence of mantras, which is of the nature of *śakti*, first resides in the subject (*pramātṛ*), then in the sense organ called the mind (*manas*), afterwards in the locations beginning with the heart, then on the tongue in the form of phonemes (*varṇa*), and immediately after that on the tip of the tongue in the form of mantras.

Such is the sequence of the emergence of *śakti*. Dissolution occurs by way of the reverse sequence. Regarding the passage beginning with "śakti": a single *prāṇāyāma* is one breath. By means of that single breath, there is the "single measure" (*ekamātrā*) spoken of by Śiva; that is, the measure previously mentioned, which is limited to a hundred—that is, measured by the number of hundreds. "Possession" (*āveśa*) is the immersion into *śakti*. This refers to the aforementioned *śakti*, who is the goddess Amarakāriṇī, the mother of the gods.

The word "possession" (*āveśa*) is understood to carry over [from the previous context]. He states the common location for the meditation on the Power (*śakti*) with the words "the birth-place" (*prasūtī*). Between the birth-place (*sūti*) and the anus (*pāna*), that is, between the genitals and the anus, lies the root-support (*mūlādhāra*) which is the womb (*yoni*). As it has been said: "The womb is between the anus and the genitals; one should contract it and hold it firm. The connection is: "the Power situated in that place. Then, having contracted from that place and having caused her to rise upward by obstructing the downward flow. And it has been said:
Then, the contraction of the anus obstructed the winds of the nine gates,
just as a jar with its mouth covered blocks the other apertures of its interior.
Thus, by the process of revolving like a wheel, he was gradually and slowly carried away through the forest.
